title: Is it possible to brainwash someone?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore whether brainwashing is real, starting with a cult-hysteria discussion and the origins of the term in Edward Hunter's 1953 book on Chinese Communist brainwashing techniques. They distinguish brainwashing (empirically linked to torture) from coercive persuasion, outline Robert J. Lifton's three-phase process (breaking down the self, possibility of salvation, rebuilding the self) with a playful role-play, discuss Korean War POW brainwashing, Mao's thought reform, and resistance techniques. They close with famous cases (Patty Hurst, Lee Boyd Malvo, the U.S. v. Fishman scientology insanity plea) and listener mail.

segments.title: Opening banter and cult hysteria
segments.summary: Josh jokingly threatens to brainwash Chuck, then they discuss cult members they know and the 1970s hysteria over cults such as the Moonies and Jim Jones's church.

segments.title: Brainwashing vs. coercive persuasion
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish brainwashing, which is linked to torture, from coercive persuasion, which works without violence and is not empirically demonstrated. They note cult members' willingness is often overlooked.

segments.title: Edward Hunter and the origins of the term
segments.summary: Edward Hunter, an anti-communist journalist, wrote a 1953 book on Red China's brainwashing techniques and testified before the McCarthy committee, popularizing fears of communist brainwashing.

segments.title: Korean War POWs and Mao's thought reform
segments.summary: Chinese and Korean captors systematically brainwashed American POWs alongside torture; about twenty-one soldiers refused repatriation, though some dispute whether they were brainwashed. Mao described thought reform (ssu xiang gai zao) in his Little Red Book, and the hosts note it is a twentieth-century phenomenon.

segments.title: Social influence and the target and agent
segments.summary: Brainwashing is based on social influence, which spans compliance, persuasion, and education (propaganda). Brainwashing combines these taken to an extreme, typically with torture, sleep deprivation, and isolation.

segments.title: Lifton's three phases in a comedic role-play
segments.summary: Lifton's three phases are outlined: breaking down the self, introducing the possibility of salvation, and rebuilding the self. The hosts illustrate them in a playful role-play in which Josh turns Chuck from a hipster into a preppy, covering attacks, disorientation via a fake birthday party, guilt, confession, and rebuilding.

segments.title: Susceptibility, resistance, and real-world parallels
segments.summary: Josh recounts a New Age convention where people seemed to attach to anything. They note susceptibility depends on weak identity, guilt, black-and-white thinking, and self-doubt. Soldiers are trained to recognize brainwashing steps; focusing on home details and a higher power is said to help resist it.

segments.title: Famous cases and legal skepticism
segments.summary: The hosts cover Patty Hearst, whose brainwashing defense failed and whose sentence was commuted by Carter, and Lee Boyd Malvo, whose attorneys suggested brainwashing. They explain that the 1990s U.S. v. Fishman case, a Scientology-linked insanity plea, effectively ended the courts' acceptance of coercive persuasion.

segments.title: Listener mail
segments.summary: Listener mail about Esperanto from Tim via Ben, and a listener's idea for a DNA-specific killer virus. Hosts also plug the Innovations podcast.
